newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - PHILIPS CUTS GRUNDIG STAKE TO 5 PCT.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - PHILIPS CUTS GRUNDIG STAKE TO 5 PCT.

text.p: Philips Electronics NV said on Friday it was cutting its 31.6 percent stake in Grundig to five percent, distancing itself yet further from the struggling German television and audio equipment maker.
A Philips spokesman said the move followed on from the company's decision at the beginning of this year to stop covering Grundig's losses and move to a passive shareholding.
"Taking into account the decision we took at the beginning of the year, it is a logical further step to reduce our interest in Grundig," said Philips spokesman Ben Geerts.

Philips added it was disputing the 671 million mark 1996 losses reported by Grundig. It said the stated loss had been inflated by extensive provisions for new policies adopted after the year end. This view was shared by a report from Arthur Andersen, but Philips had not reached a settlement with Grundig.
"Philips will therefore request the court to nullify Grundig's 1996 Annual Accounts," Philips said.
Philips said it had sold the 26.6 percent stake to an investor group led by privately owned London based merchant bank firm Botts and Company Limited.
"The consideration of the shares depends on the realisable future value thereof," Philips said in a statement.
It added Botts had also bought a 16.4 percent stake of Grundig shares held by German asset management firm Hohenstaufen Vierundvierzigste Vermogensverwaltung GmbH.

At the heart of Philips' troubled relationship with Grundig is a deal struck in 1984 in which Philips agreed to pay an annual dividend to Grundig and to buy 52 percent of the company for 411 million marks in 2004.
"We won't take the initiative to reopen negotiations. That means that in 2004, they will execute their put option to sell the 52 percent to us. We would sell it further," said Geerts.
"They have the right to exercise their put option in 2004, we tried to get a settlement but without success," he added.

"As from the beginning of this year we became a passive minority shareholder and we're still in that position with five percent. We continue to view Grundig as a valued business partner, only we have conflicts about the magnitude of the 1996 losses," Geerts said.

Analysts welcomed the move by Philips to tackle one of its principal loss-makers -- part of the strategy kicked off by chairman Cor Boonstra when he vowed late last year to deal with "bleeders" and underperformers.

"They're slowly making progress with solving this Grundig problem, but they still have five percent and they still have the obligation to buy the 52 percent in 2004 and pay the annual dividend," said ING Barings analyst Steven Vrolijk.
"Philips made provisions last year to cover problems with Grundig but, from the company's point of view, it's still a cash outflow, it still takes up management time," he said.
"The fact that they're saying they will contest the Grundig annual report in court is probably not doing them much good in the German market," Vrolijk added.
Philips shares were down 0.50 guilders to 156.60 guilders in a mixed and volatile Amsterdam share market. The shares reached an all-time high of 162.50 guilders on Thursday.
